doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Jump Town and the Ventura band
title: Working out vocalese: syllables, precision and Ruth Price's charts
summary: How they find horn-like syllables, stay precise, early silly scat attempts, and Ruth Price copying Ventura's syllable charts.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you sit at the piano when you do that? “I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles.” Do you sit at the piano and kind of flesh out an idea or do you mostly just think about it?

No. I play it and listen for things. And that’s where the, like when we do this vocalese section. That’s where the improvisation comes in, where I’m [scats] — and I say oh yeah, yeah. Oh change this a little bit, okay.
You kind of play it over and over and over and go over it until an idea occurs to you, and then you experiment with it.

Because to have it sound right, the two of us have to be exact, and it’s like if two tap dancers were to dance together, and they’re doing two different things, it would be chop suey. So we have to be precise and do the same things, in fact use the same syllables.
For the most part, but not always, because we go into harmony when we do it, but I mean basically when you do the things together, it’s nice.
Did you ever have occasion when you started writing, obviously at some point you had to write the scat down?
Because how do you spell, let’s see now [scats]

Yeah. You know the funny thing is we go over it and we try to find the sound that’s the closest to what a horn would sound like, where the accents come and things, like if it was a trumpet going dup du ah. So you think dup du ah. You have to sing an open sound.
Or we do, like when we do the thing, du da — du da — du da.
Yeah. You try to duplicate the closest thing you can with the voice.

But in the beginning we had some pretty funny ones I must admit. Like we did a tune of Roy’s called “Euphoria” which was based on the changes of “S’Wonderful.” And it was pretty [scats]. I mean we had some [scats] and now it sounds dumb to us. But I remember one time we were working in a club in San Francisco and some guy who was going to college there came up and he was sitting there writing most every night and I thought what the heck is he doing? And he was making a survey on how many times we sang certain vowels and how we were trying — and when he questioned us we said gee I don’t know, we don’t figure it out to that degree.
I never count how much you sing them. But here’s a funny one. We left Ventura at the end of 1949. Then Ruth Price, who runs the Jazz Bakery out in Los Angeles and is doing © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

very well with it, is also a singer. She joined Ventura after we left, and she said that he had her write down all the syllables on long butcher paper, just sheets of it. And she said she would have it hanging on the walls anywhere she could see it so she could do these charts the same way. And I said, “Oh Ruth, that’s terrible to have to do that. Why don’t you just make up your own?” She says, “no, he wanted just like it was on the original.

And she probably wasn’t used to doing that at that point you know, because she wasn’t singing vocalese. And we’d been doing it. Now it’s easy. Now when we do just an arrangement we sit down and the right thing sort of comes. Once in a while we’ll quibble over you know, we each have a different viewpoint, but then it always comes down to which one works best. But we sort of more or less sing it and fall right into it now. So it’s easier.
